title: Y-R-A
hookLine: yirah means both fear and awe

cards: Jacob is running from his brother. Night falls on the road, and he lies down with a stone under his head. He dreams of a ladder set on the earth, its top reaching to heaven, and angels going up and down on it.
Then he wakes on the same hard ground and says: "Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not." And the very next words: "And he was afraid, and said, How dreadful is this place!" Afraid.
Dreadful. Two English words, and in the Hebrew, both come from today's three letters.

teach.b: Y-R-A. Yod, resh, alef. Yirah: fear, and awe.
Four scenes. First, Jacob. He was afraid, vayira, and the place was dreadful, nora.
He doesn't flee this place; he's shaken by it, and calls it "none other but the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven." Second, wisdom.

A psalm says: "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom." Some readers hear yirah there less as terror and more as the right kind of smallness: knowing the world is bigger than you, and that you are not its center.

At the sea, after the crossing, Exodus says: "and the people feared the LORD, and believed the LORD, and his servant Moses." Believed is a form of A-M-N, the root of steadiness from earlier this block.
Fear and faith stand side by side. Fourth, how awe begins.
Maimonides, in his Mishneh Torah, writes that when a person looks closely at the great and wondrous works of creation, love rises first, a longing to know.
Right after, the person draws back, aware of how small and brief they are. That's yirah: fear that stays to look.
The days from Rosh Hashanah to Yom Kippur are called the Yamim Noraim, the Days of Awe, from the same root as Jacob's dreadful place.

how: The days from Rosh Hashanah through Yom Kippur are called the Days of Awe, and Jewish prayer books carry blessings for moments of wonder, such as seeing lightning or a great sea.

o: fear and awe, held together in one root
plain terror, the urge to run and hide
worship, the act of bowing before God

games.q: fear and awe — tap the pairs.

s: the same root carries awe: Jacob's 'dreadful' place is the house of God.
at the sea, the people feared the LORD and believed
Exodus puts fear and faith side by side.
for Maimonides, awe comes with no love at all
he describes love rising first, then a drawing back in awe.

games.q: you're Jacob. you've woken on the road from a dream of a ladder to heaven, shaken. it's morning. what do you do?
o: leave quickly and never speak of it.
set up your stone pillow as a pillar and name the place.
lie down again to try to dream it twice.
games.why: Jacob sets up the stone as a pillar, pours oil on it, and names the place Bethel, house of God. awe made him mark the spot.

practice: Choose something close by and look at it as if for the first time: your own hand, its lines and joints, the fact that it moves when you ask; or the sky through a window; or your breath, coming in without being called.
Stay with it until it gets a little strange, a little large, and let yourself be small next to it. If you pray, you can say Jacob's words: surely the LORD is in this place.

wordCard.voice: Y-R-A. Yod, resh, alef: fear and awe in one root. Jacob's dreadful place, and the Days of Awe. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: fear and awe; from the root yod, resh, alef.

carryVoice: Your line: awe. Yirah is the kind of fear that stays to look. Until tomorrow.
